# Skill: Spring Boot Cache Redis Guardrails

## Goal
Ship Spring Cache on Redis (including Azure Cache for Redis) that expires on purpose, serializes safely, isolates keys per app and environment, and stays correct when more than one pod is running.

## When to apply
- Enabling `spring-boot-starter-cache` with Redis, or reviewing an existing `CacheManager`
- Adding or changing `@Cacheable`, `@CacheEvict`, or `@CachePut`
- Incidents with stale data, unbounded Redis memory, stampedes, or cross-pod inconsistency
- Moving a local or container Redis onto Azure Cache for Redis
- Hardening serializers, key names, or bulk eviction before production

## Baseline rules
1. **Select Redis explicitly and keep caching off slice tests.** Depend on `spring-boot-starter-cache` and `spring-boot-starter-data-redis` (Lettuce unless the build already chose Jedis). Set `spring.cache.type=redis`. Do not assume "Redis on the classpath" picks the right manager when another provider is present. Put `@EnableCaching` on a dedicated `@Configuration` (for example `RedisCacheConfig`), not on `@SpringBootApplication`. `@WebMvcTest` and `@DataJpaTest` load the application class; they do not component-scan an arbitrary `@Configuration`. Leaving `@EnableCaching` on the application class pulls cache advice and a connection into slices that should stay light.
2. **Every cache has a TTL.** `RedisCacheConfiguration` defaults to `Duration.ZERO`, which means entries never expire. That grows memory without bound and, on a server policy of `noeviction`, turns a full cache into write errors. Set a global floor with `spring.cache.redis.time-to-live`. Prefer per-cache TTL through a `RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer` that calls `withCacheConfiguration` and `entryTtl`. Start from the auto-configured `RedisCacheConfiguration` bean so prefix, null policy, and serializer stay intact. Do not replace `CacheManager` with a hand-built bean, and do not declare your own `RedisCacheConfiguration` `@Bean`, unless you re-apply `CacheProperties` yourself. Both bypasses drop Boot's `spring.cache.redis.*` binding (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`).
3. **JSON values, string keys, explicit types.** Boot's default value serializer is JDK serialization: opaque bytes, brittle across class moves, and awkward to inspect. Prefer a typed `Jackson2JsonRedisSerializer` when a cache stores one concrete DTO. Use `GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer` only with an `ObjectMapper` whose polymorphic validator allowlists those DTOs. Permissive default typing (`@class` plus a laissez-faire subtype validator) is a deserialization risk if anything besides this app can write the keyspace. Document the allowlist. Serialize keys with a string serializer so prefixes and ids stay readable. Do not cache JPA entities, credentials, or types outside the allowlist.
4. **Prefix and namespace every key.** Leave `spring.cache.redis.use-key-prefix=true` (the default). Turning it off lets two cache names share one Redis key. Set `spring.cache.redis.key-prefix` to application name, environment, and a schema version (`orders:prod:v3:`). Shared Azure instances must not mix apps or environments. Use stable SpEL (`key = "#id"`) that you repeat on evict and put. The default key generator hashes every argument, so `Pageable`, principals, and `toString()` of entities become huge or sensitive keys. Never put secrets, tokens, passwords, emails, national ids, or other raw PII in keys or values. Keys show up in `SCAN`, slow logs, and Azure diagnostics.
5. **Evict one key. Do not `KEYS` the instance.** Prefer `@CacheEvict` / `@CachePut` with the same key the read path uses. `allEntries = true` and `Cache.clear()` walk the keyspace. `RedisCacheManager.builder(connectionFactory)` uses a non-locking writer whose batch strategy is `KEYS` in current Spring Data Redis. `KEYS` is blocking and is a poor fit for a large Azure keyspace. For a real bulk drop, either configure `RedisCacheWriter` with `BatchStrategies.scan(batchSize)` (still expensive, non-atomic, per node on cluster) or bump the version segment of the key prefix and let TTL reap the old generation. Do not call `FLUSHDB` or `FLUSHALL` from application code.
6. **Decide nulls, then decide stampede.** Default `spring.cache.redis.cache-null-values=true` stores nulls for the full TTL (forever, if TTL was left at zero). Pick one policy: `unless = "#result == null"` and disable null caching, or a dedicated short-TTL cache for negative lookups. `disableCachingNullValues()` without `unless` throws when a method returns null, because the cache still attempts the put. `condition` runs before invocation (skip lookup and store). `unless` runs after (the method always runs; the result might not be stored), so it does not stop a stampede. `@Cacheable(sync = true)` locks inside one JVM only. Boot's writer is non-locking, so it is not cross-pod single-flight. If you add a Redis lock, document the lock key, the lock TTL, and the outcome when the holder dies (callers fall through to the database, or they fail).
7. **Write the system of record, then the cache.** Keep the default `beforeInvocation = false` so evict/put runs after a successful method. Evicting first lets a concurrent reader reload the pre-write row and pin it until TTL. `transactionAware()` on the manager builder defers put/evict until after commit. Boot does not enable it. Turn it on only when a rolled-back transaction must not change the cache. Same-transaction reads will not see the deferred write, and a crash after commit but before the sync leaves stale data until TTL. Assume every pod shares one Redis. A process-local cache (Caffeine) is not coherent across pods. Do not add a near cache unless invalidation is designed and tested. `sync = true` does not coordinate pods.
8. **Choose fail-open or fail-closed on purpose.** Set `spring.data.redis.timeout` below the caller's timeout so a stuck command does not pin the worker pool. Lettuce pooling needs `commons-pool2` and `spring.data.redis.lettuce.pool.*` (including `max-wait`); an unbounded wait hides the outage. The default `SimpleCacheErrorHandler` rethrows, so a Redis miss-path error fails the request even when the database could answer. That is fail-closed. For fail-open reads, a `CacheErrorHandler` that logs `handleCacheGetError` and does not rethrow lets the interceptor run the method. Swallowing put/evict errors hides a failed invalidation until TTL. Read-mostly catalogs can fail open. Authorization and idempotency keys should fail closed. When Actuator is on the classpath, Redis health is available; do not publish health details on the public port. Use a remote cache when pods must observe the same eviction. Use a local cache when per-pod staleness is acceptable and a Redis outage must not matter.
9. **Test without a live Redis, then test the hot path with one.** Unit and slice tests should not open a socket. With `@EnableCaching` isolated, `@WebMvcTest` does not cache. Where a slice needs the abstraction, use `@AutoConfigureCache` or `spring.cache.type=none` and assert outcomes, not Redis bytes. For integration of hit, miss, eviction, and null policy, use Testcontainers with a pinned image (for example `redis:7-alpine`), `@ServiceConnection` on Boot 3.1+, or dynamic host/port properties. Do not point CI at Azure or a shared dev cache. Include a round-trip that fails if values come back as JDK payload when JSON was required.
10. **Azure Cache for Redis is still Redis, plus network and identity.** Enable TLS (`spring.data.redis.ssl.enabled=true`) and use the instance hostname and TLS port (commonly 6380 when non-TLS is disabled). Prefer Microsoft Entra authentication where that tier and the client stack already in the repo support short-lived data-plane tokens. Otherwise set `spring.data.redis.password` from the environment or the app's existing Key Vault reference. Never commit access keys, connection strings, or primary/secondary secrets, and do not invent secret names or resource ids. Restrict the network with the firewall or a private endpoint and private DNS; laptops use local Redis or an approved tunnel, not the production key on a public endpoint. Application TTLs still matter if the server policy is `noeviction`. Use cluster configuration only when the instance is clustered, and do not assume a multi-key command spans prefixes.

## Tool placement
- **GitHub Copilot:** path-scoped `.github/instructions/spring-boot-cache-redis.instructions.md` with `applyTo` covering the cache configuration class, `application*.{yml,yaml,properties}`, and files that declare `@Cacheable`, `@CacheEvict`, or `@CachePut`. Keep one always-on line in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: Redis caches have a TTL, JSON values, a namespaced prefix, and no `allEntries=true` on large keyspaces.
- **Claude Code:** procedure in `.claude/skills/spring-boot-cache-redis-guardrails/SKILL.md`. One CLAUDE.md fact: "Spring Cache on Redis always sets a TTL via RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer; @EnableCaching lives on an isolated @Configuration, not the application class."
- **Codex:** a short cache section in root `AGENTS.md`, or `docs/agents/spring-boot-cache-redis.md` linked from it when the root file would grow. State TTL, serializer, prefix, eviction, and fail-open versus fail-closed.

## Anti-patterns
- `@EnableCaching` on `@SpringBootApplication`, so every slice test opens Redis
- Leaving TTL unset and treating "it works on my laptop" as production-safe
- A custom `CacheManager` or `RedisCacheConfiguration` bean that silently ignores `spring.cache.redis.*`
- JDK-serialized values, or JSON with permissive `@class` typing on a shared cache
- `use-key-prefix=false`, or one prefix shared by dev and prod
- SpEL built from `toString()`, tokens, or PII
- `@CacheEvict(allEntries = true)` as a routine invalidation on Azure-sized keyspaces
- `disableCachingNullValues()` without `unless`, so legitimate null returns throw
- Believing `sync = true` is a cluster-wide single-flight
- Evicting before the database write, or assuming transaction-aware cache is on by default
- A Caffeine near cache with no invalidation story in a multi-pod deployment
- Fail-open put/evict on data that must not stay stale past the method return
- CI tests aimed at a shared Redis or at Azure
- Access keys, connection strings, or firewall exceptions committed "just for local"

## Verification
- [ ] `spring.cache.type=redis` and both starters are present; `@EnableCaching` is not on the application class
- [ ] Global TTL is set, and each hot cache has an explicit TTL from `RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer` derived from Boot's configuration
- [ ] No replacement `CacheManager` / `RedisCacheConfiguration` bean drops Boot properties
- [ ] Values are JSON with a documented type allowlist; keys are strings; prefix includes app, environment, and schema version
- [ ] Read and evict SpEL keys match; keys and values contain no secrets or PII
- [ ] Bulk clear is scan-based or version-bumped; `allEntries=true` is absent on large caches
- [ ] Null policy is explicit (`unless` / `condition` / short null TTL) and does not throw on ordinary nulls
- [ ] Cross-pod single-flight, if any, documents lock TTL and the failure mode; `sync=true` is not described as cluster-wide
- [ ] Write-then-evict order is intact; `transactionAware` is set only if the PR explains it
- [ ] Command timeout, pool wait, and `CacheErrorHandler` match the chosen fail-open or fail-closed mode
- [ ] Slice tests do not need Redis; hot-path integration uses a pinned Testcontainers image
- [ ] Azure notes name TLS, auth source (Entra or access key via env/Key Vault), and private network, with no secrets in the diff

## Copy-ready SKILL.md stub

---
name: spring-boot-cache-redis-guardrails
description: Use when designing or reviewing Spring Cache on Redis or Azure Cache for Redis — TTL via RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer, JSON serializers, key prefixes, eviction, stampede, and multi-pod correctness.
---

Follow Spring Boot Cache Redis Guardrails: explicit redis cache type, @EnableCaching on an isolated configuration, TTL on every cache, JSON values, namespaced prefixes, targeted eviction, and a documented fail-open or fail-closed policy.
```

# Skill: Maven Multi-Module CI Cache Guardrails

## Goal
Make GitHub Actions builds for a Maven multi-module reactor fast and correct: cache the local repository by pom hashes, keep the reactor deterministic, and never poison the cache with `target/` output or secrets.

## When to apply
- Adding or reviewing `setup-java` / `actions/cache` for a Maven monorepo
- Slow CI after new modules, BOM bumps, or snapshot churn
- Flaky builds that pass locally but fail after a cache hit
- Introducing `-T` parallel reactor builds or selective module builds (`-pl` / `-am` / `-amd`)
- Hardening cache keys, restore-keys, and path lists before production pipelines

## Baseline rules
1. **Prefer `setup-java` Maven cache over a hand-rolled `actions/cache`.** On GitHub-hosted runners, `actions/setup-java` with `cache: maven` hashes the dependency tree from the poms and restores `~/.m2/repository`. Use it unless the workflow already has a documented custom cache (for example a shared self-hosted cache layout). If you must use `actions/cache` directly, pin the action major, set `path` to `~/.m2/repository` only, and key on OS plus a hash of every `pom.xml` (and the Maven wrapper props if the wrapper pins the distribution).
2. **Key on every pom that can change the classpath.** In a multi-module reactor the parent BOM, dependencyManagement, and pluginManagement all affect resolution. Hash `**/pom.xml` (or the concrete list the root reactor includes). Include `.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties` when the wrapper is the source of truth for the Maven version. Do not key only on the root pom — a leaf module bump must bust the cache.
3. **Never cache `**/target` or compiled classes.** Module `target/` directories are build outputs. Caching them across jobs mixes stale class files with new sources and causes ghost test failures. Cache the local repository (resolved jars) and rebuild modules each run. If you need artifact reuse between jobs in one workflow, use `actions/upload-artifact` / `download-artifact` for specific jars, not a persistent `target/` cache key.
4. **Keep restore-keys as a fallback prefix, not a second full key.** A typical pattern is `key: ${{ runner.os }}-m2-${{ hashFiles('**/pom.xml') }}` with `restore-keys: ${{ runner.os }}-m2-`. A partial restore is fine (extra jars stay; missing ones download). Do not use an overly broad key that never changes — that freezes an old dependency set after a BOM bump until manual eviction.
5. **Use the Maven Wrapper in CI.** Commit `.mvn/wrapper` and invoke `./mvnw` (or `mvnw.cmd` on Windows) so the Maven version matches developers. Pin `distributionUrl` to a release, not a moving `latest`. Do not install a different Maven via apt and ignore the wrapper when the repo has one.
6. **CI-friendly Maven flags are mandatory.** Always pass `-B` (batch) and prefer `-ntp` (no transfer progress). Fail the job on dependency warnings that hide resolution problems when the team already treats them as errors (`-Dorg.slf4j.simpleLogger.log.org.apache.maven.cli.transfer.Slf4jMavenTransferListener=warn` is optional noise control, not a substitute for `-B`). Do not hide test failures with blanket `-DskipTests` on the main verify job; use a dedicated job or profile only when the pipeline already separates compile from test.
7. **Reactor flags for multi-module: be explicit.** Default CI should run from the reactor root: `./mvnw -B -ntp verify` (or the project's standard lifecycle). Selective builds with `-pl module-a,module-b -am` are for PR paths when the workflow already computes the affected modules; document how the module list is derived. `-amd` builds dependents; use it when an API module change must re-test consumers. Do not combine ad-hoc `-pl` with a stale local repo assumption — the cache must still contain the parent BOM artifacts.
8. **Parallel builds need thread-safe plugins.** `-T 1C` (one thread per core) or `-T 2` can cut wall time on large reactors. Confirm surefire/failsafe fork settings and any custom plugins are safe under concurrent module builds. If a module is known unsafe, exclude it from parallelism or keep CI serial until fixed. Document the chosen `-T` value in the workflow comment or AGENTS.md.
9. **Snapshots and mirror config belong in checked-in settings — carefully.** If CI uses a `settings.xml` (company mirror, authenticated registry), mount it via `actions/setup-java` `server-id` / env-backed passwords or a short-lived token. Never commit passwords, tokens, or base64-encoded credentials. Prefer OIDC or short-lived cloud tokens already used elsewhere in the repo over long-lived `settings.xml` secrets. Snapshot updates (`-U`) belong on a scheduled or main-branch job when snapshot deps exist; do not force `-U` on every PR unless the team depends on floating snapshots (prefer pinning).
10. **Separate dependency resolution from tests when it helps.** A common pattern: job 1 resolves and optionally runs `./mvnw -B -ntp -DskipTests package` with cache save; job 2 restores the same cache key and runs tests. With `setup-java` cache, a single job that runs `verify` is enough for most repos — only split when wall time or runners justify it. Post-job cache save failures must not hide a red test step; keep test exit code authoritative.
11. **Windows vs Ubuntu runners.** Cache keys must include `runner.os` (or an explicit OS label). Path separators and the wrapper script differ; use `./mvnw` on Unix and `mvnw.cmd` on Windows, or `bash mvnw` when bash is available. Do not assume a Linux-only `~/.m2` path on Windows runners (`~/.m2/repository` still works under the user home, but document it).
12. **Validate locally before trusting CI cache lore.** Reproduce with `./mvnw -B -ntp -o verify` (offline) after a populated local repo to confirm the reactor does not need unexpected remote hits. In CI logs, confirm cache restore HIT/MISS and that dependency downloads after a pom-only change are expected. Watch for cache thrash: keys that change every run (embedding `github.sha` into the m2 key) defeat the purpose.

## Tool placement
- **GitHub Copilot:** path-scoped `.github/instructions/maven-ci-cache.instructions.md` with `applyTo` for `**/pom.xml`, `.github/workflows/**/*.{yml,yaml}`, and `**/.mvn/**`. One always-on line in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: CI caches `~/.m2/repository` keyed by hashed poms; never cache `**/target`.
- **Claude Code:** procedure in `.claude/skills/maven-multimodule-ci-cache-guardrails/SKILL.md`. One CLAUDE.md fact: "Maven CI uses setup-java cache or actions/cache on ~/.m2/repository keyed by **/pom.xml; never cache target/."
- **Codex:** short Maven CI section in root `AGENTS.md`, or `docs/agents/maven-ci-cache.md` linked from it. State cache path, key inputs, wrapper, and reactor command.

## Anti-patterns
- Caching `**/target` or the whole workspace as a "speedup"
- Keying the m2 cache only on the root pom in a multi-module tree
- Embedding `github.sha` or a timestamp into the dependency cache key
- Ignoring the Maven Wrapper and installing a different Maven in CI
- Blanket `-DskipTests` on the only verify job to "make cache warmer"
- Committing `settings.xml` with passwords or tokens
- Assuming `-T` is safe without checking surefire forks / custom plugins
- Partial `-pl` builds without `-am` when the module needs reactor siblings
- restore-keys so broad they keep serving a pre-CVE dependency set with no pom hash change path
- Documenting Azure/GitHub secrets or mirror URLs that are not already in the repo

## Verification
- [ ] Workflow uses `setup-java` `cache: maven` or an equivalent `actions/cache` on `~/.m2/repository` only
- [ ] Cache key hashes all relevant `pom.xml` files (and wrapper props if used)
- [ ] No path entry caches `**/target` or compiled outputs across runs
- [ ] CI invokes `./mvnw` (or documented Windows equivalent) with `-B` and preferably `-ntp`
- [ ] Default job runs a full reactor verify (or a documented selective `-pl/-am` strategy)
- [ ] Parallel `-T` is documented and known-safe for this repo, or omitted
- [ ] No credentials in committed settings; tokens via env / OIDC already used in-repo
- [ ] After a leaf pom dependency bump, CI shows cache miss or partial restore then downloads the new artifact
- [ ] Offline local `./mvnw -B -ntp -o verify` works on a warm machine for the same revision

## Copy-ready SKILL.md stub

---
name: maven-multimodule-ci-cache-guardrails
description: Use when speeding up or reviewing GitHub Actions Maven multi-module builds — setup-java/m2 cache keys, reactor flags, wrapper, and never caching target/.
---

Follow Maven Multi-Module CI Cache Guardrails: cache ~/.m2/repository keyed by hashed poms, use the Maven Wrapper with -B -ntp, never cache **/target, and document any -pl/-am or -T usage.
```

# Skill: Kubernetes Probes & Graceful Shutdown Guardrails

## Goal
Make Kubernetes rollouts safe for HTTP services (Spring Boot first-class, generic apps welcome): correct startup/liveness/readiness probes, coordinated graceful shutdown, and no cascading restarts from dependency blips.

## When to apply
- New Deployments/Helm charts for Spring Boot or other HTTP services on AKS/Kubernetes
- Rolling updates that drop in-flight requests (502/connection resets) or restart under load
- Reviews of probe paths, thresholds, `preStop`, and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
- Apps enabling Actuator health groups or moving probes to a management port
- Slow-starting JVMs killed before they become ready

## Baseline rules
1. **Three probes, three jobs.** `startupProbe` protects slow boot; until it succeeds, liveness/readiness are not evaluated. `livenessProbe` answers “should Kubernetes restart this process?” — keep it cheap and local. `readinessProbe` answers “should this Pod receive traffic?” — dependencies and warm-up belong here. Do not collapse all three onto `/actuator/health` without groups.
2. **Prefer dedicated health groups for Spring Boot.** Enable probes (`management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true` on supported Boot versions) and point HTTP probes at `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` (adjust for `management.endpoints.web.base-path`). Keep the liveness group free of DB/Redis/broker checks; put those on readiness (or custom indicators used only by readiness). For non-Spring apps, expose a lightweight `/livez` (process up) and `/readyz` (deps + accept traffic).
3. **Probe the port that serves the app path you care about.** If Actuator runs on a separate `management.server.port`, probes must use that `containerPort` (and the Deployment must declare it). Avoid a probe that succeeds on the management port while the main listener is down — document the chosen layout. Endpoint *exposure* and auth belong in the actuator hardening skill; here the rule is: probes must hit a stable, privately reachable path that reflects the AvailabilityState you intend.
4. **Always add a startupProbe for JVM services with non-trivial boot.** Example shape: HTTP GET to the liveness (or readiness) path, `periodSeconds: 5`, `failureThreshold` sized so `period × failureThreshold` covers p99 cold start (often 60–180s). Prefer startupProbe over large `initialDelaySeconds` on liveness. After startup succeeds, keep liveness/readiness `initialDelaySeconds` small or zero.
5. **Tune failureThreshold and periodSeconds deliberately.** Defaults (`periodSeconds: 10`, `timeoutSeconds: 1`) are often too tight under GC or brief CPU throttle. Typical production bands: readiness `periodSeconds: 5–10`, `failureThreshold: 2–3`, `timeoutSeconds: 1–3`; liveness slightly slower (`periodSeconds: 10–15`, `failureThreshold: 3+`) so a single slow request does not restart the Pod. Document the math in a chart comment when thresholds are non-default.
6. **Enable graceful shutdown in the app.** For Spring Boot: `server.shutdown=graceful` and a bounded `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` (for example `30s`) so in-flight requests finish and readiness flips to refusing traffic. Ensure the process receives SIGTERM (PID 1 or a signal-forwarding entrypoint — no shell wrapper that swallows signals). Non-Spring: drain the HTTP server on SIGTERM with an explicit timeout.
7. **Close the endpoint-propagation race with `preStop`.** Kubernetes can send SIGTERM while kube-proxy/EndpointSlice updates are still catching up. Add a `lifecycle.preStop` sleep (commonly `sleep 10`–`15`, or an exec that waits briefly) *before* the app starts draining, so new traffic stops arriving. Keep the sleep boring and deterministic; do not run complex scripts that can hang.
8. **Fit the whole drain inside `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.** Budget: `preStop sleep + app shutdown timeout + small buffer` ≤ `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (often 45–90s for HTTP APIs). If the grace period is shorter than the sleep + lifecycle timeout, Kubernetes sends SIGKILL and you lose the graceful path. Align Deployment, PodDisruptionBudget expectations, and HPA scale-in with the same budget.
9. **Rollout and mesh awareness.** During RollingUpdate, `maxUnavailable`/`maxSurge` plus readiness must keep enough Ready Pods. If you use a service mesh or ingress with long idle timeouts, ensure readiness failure removes the Pod from backends before preStop finishes. Do not rely on liveness to “fix” overload — fix capacity or readiness instead.
10. **Observe probe failures as first-class signals.** Watch `kube_pod_container_status_restarts`, Ready condition flaps, and application readiness state transitions. A spike in liveness failures is an incident; a readiness flap during a dependency outage can be correct behavior. Alert on restart loops, not on every readiness failure.

## Checklist
- [ ] Distinct startup / liveness / readiness (or documented reason for omitting startup)
- [ ] Liveness path has no remote dependency checks
- [ ] Readiness reflects “accept traffic” (deps, warm-up, migrations finished)
- [ ] Probe port/path match Actuator or custom livez/readyz layout
- [ ] startupProbe failure budget covers cold start; liveness not used as a fake startup delay
- [ ] `server.shutdown=graceful` (or equivalent) + bounded shutdown phase timeout
- [ ] `preStop` sleep present; SIGTERM reaches the JVM/process
- [ ] `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` ≥ preStop + shutdown timeout + buffer
- [ ] RollingUpdate / PDB still leave enough Ready Pods
- [ ] Actuator exposure reviewed separately (no public management LoadBalancer)

## Anti-patterns
- Liveness pointing at `/actuator/health` with DB/disk/mail indicators — DB blip restarts the fleet
- No startupProbe and a huge `initialDelaySeconds` that delays failure detection forever after the first start
- Aggressive liveness (`timeoutSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`) under load or GC
- Graceful shutdown enabled but `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` left at 30s with a 30s app timeout and a 15s preStop (SIGKILL)
- `preStop` that calls the app’s own `/shutdown` without coordinating readiness, or a hook that can block past the grace period
- Probes against a public Ingress URL instead of the container port
- Shell entrypoint (`java ... & wait`) that never forwards SIGTERM

## Verification
1. `kubectl describe pod` / events: startup succeeds; no unexpected liveness kills during boot.
2. Exec or port-forward: liveness returns UP while artificially breaking a dependency; readiness goes DOWN.
3. Trigger a rollout: confirm in-flight requests complete (no surge of 502s) and Pods leave Ready before process exit.
4. Confirm process exit within grace period (no `Kill` after exceeded grace in events).
5. Chaos: brief DB outage → readiness flaps, restart count stays flat.

## Copilot / Claude Code / Codex notes
- Copilot: keep applyTo narrow to manifests and `application*.{yml,yaml,properties}`; paste the checklist into the PR description.
- Claude Code: SKILL.md holds this procedure; CLAUDE.md only stores the one-liner on probe roles + grace budget.
- Codex: put the budget formula and anti-patterns in AGENTS.md; ask for a small Deployment/values + application config diff only.

# Skill: Spring Boot Structured Logging Guardrails

## Goal
Logs that are machine-parseable, correlated with traces, cheap at volume, and safe to ship off-cluster.

## When to apply
- New Spring Boot services or containers headed to AKS/Kubernetes
- Reviews touching `log.*` calls, `logback-spring.xml`, or `logging.*` properties
- Incidents where logs could not be searched, joined to a trace, or leaked sensitive data

## Baseline rules
1. **JSON on stdout in containers.** On Spring Boot 3.4+ prefer built-in structured logging (`logging.structured.format.console=ecs` or `logstash`); on older versions use a JSON encoder in `logback-spring.xml` behind a profile. Keep human-readable pattern logs for the local profile only. Never write log files inside the container.
2. **Parameterized messages only.** `log.info("Order {} accepted", orderId)` — no string concatenation, no `String.format` in hot paths. Pass exceptions as the last argument so the stack trace is kept: `log.error("Payment failed for {}", id, ex)`.
3. **Correlation everywhere.** Every line carries `traceId`/`spanId` (Micrometer Tracing or OpenTelemetry populates MDC). Add request-scoped keys (tenant, request id) via MDC in a filter and clear them in `finally`. For `@Async`/executors, propagate context with a `TaskDecorator` or context-propagation library.
4. **Levels mean something.** ERROR = needs a human; WARN = degraded but handled; INFO = business/lifecycle events; DEBUG/TRACE off in prod by default. Do not log-and-rethrow the same exception at every layer — log once at the boundary.
5. **No secrets, tokens, or PII.** Never log `Authorization` headers, JWTs, passwords, connection strings, Key Vault values, full request/response bodies, or personal identifiers. Mask at the source (`toString()` that redacts, dedicated DTOs) rather than relying on downstream scrubbing.
6. **Bounded volume.** No logging inside tight loops; sample or rate-limit noisy paths; avoid unbounded MDC values or high-cardinality keys in message text that pipelines index.
7. **Runtime level changes are controlled.** If `/actuator/loggers` is exposed, keep it on the management port and authenticated (see spring-boot-actuator-hardening).

## Review checklist
- [ ] Container profile emits one JSON object per line on stdout
- [ ] traceId/spanId present; MDC cleared after each request
- [ ] No concatenated log messages; exceptions passed as throwable
- [ ] No tokens, secrets, or PII in any new log line (grep `Authorization`, `token`, `password`)
- [ ] Levels match the rules; prod root level is INFO or WARN
- [ ] A test or log capture (e.g. `OutputCaptureExtension`) asserts a key line is structured and redacted

## Anti-patterns
- `log.debug("payload=" + body)` in request filters
- `e.printStackTrace()` or `System.out.println`
- Catch-log-rethrow at every layer producing five copies of one stack trace
- Shipping DEBUG to Log Analytics and paying for it

# Skill: Bash Script Hardening Guardrails

## Goal
Shell scripts that fail loudly, handle any filename or input safely, clean up after themselves, and pass ShellCheck in CI.

## When to apply
- New or changed `*.sh` files, container entrypoints, or Jenkins/GitHub Actions helper scripts
- Reviews where a script silently continued after an error or broke on spaces in paths
- Incidents caused by an unset variable, a glob, or a leaked secret in `set -x` output

## Baseline rules
1. **Explicit interpreter and strict mode.** Start with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and `set -Eeuo pipefail`. If the script must be POSIX `sh`, say so and drop Bash-only features. Do not rely on strict mode alone — check exit codes where `set -e` is known not to fire (inside `if`, `&&`/`||` chains, command substitution in `local x=$(...)`).
2. **Quote every expansion.** `"$var"`, `"$@"`, `"${arr[@]}"`. Use arrays for argument lists, never word-split strings. Use `--` before user-supplied paths (`rm -- "$file"`).
3. **Safe temp files and cleanup.** `tmp=$(mktemp -d)` plus `trap 'rm -rf -- "$tmp"' EXIT`. Add an `ERR` trap that prints the failing line (`$LINENO`, `$BASH_COMMAND`) to stderr.
4. **Validate inputs up front.** Required env vars via `: "${API_URL:?API_URL is required}"`; check required binaries with `command -v`. Print usage and exit 2 on bad arguments.
5. **No secrets in output.** Never `set -x` around tokens; never echo credentials or pass them as command-line args visible in `ps` — use env vars or stdin (`--password-stdin`). Mask values in GitHub Actions with `::add-mask::`.
6. **Idempotent and safe to rerun.** `mkdir -p`, check-before-create, no destructive `rm -rf "$DIR/"` where `DIR` could be empty (guard with `:?`).
7. **Containers: exec the main process.** Entrypoints end with `exec "$@"` so signals reach the app (see k8s-probes-graceful-shutdown-guardrails).
8. **Lint and format in CI.** `shellcheck -x` with zero warnings (justify any `# shellcheck disable=SCxxxx` inline) and `shfmt -d`; add `bats` tests for non-trivial logic.

## Review checklist
- [ ] Shebang + `set -Eeuo pipefail` (or documented POSIX sh)
- [ ] All expansions quoted; arrays used for arg lists
- [ ] `mktemp` + `trap ... EXIT` for temp state
- [ ] Required env vars and tools validated with clear errors
- [ ] No secrets in `set -x`, echo, or argv
- [ ] ShellCheck and shfmt pass in CI; bats tests for branching logic

## Anti-patterns
- `for f in $(ls *.txt)` and unquoted `$1`
- `curl ... | bash` from an unpinned URL
- `cd somedir` without `|| exit` followed by `rm -rf *`
- Entrypoint that runs the app as a child so SIGTERM never arrives

# Skill: Spring Boot OpenAPI Contract Guardrails

## Goal
REST APIs whose published OpenAPI 3 document is the source of truth — request/response shapes, validation, error media type, and versioning stay aligned with the running Spring Boot code.

## When to apply
- New Spring Boot services exposing HTTP APIs, or reviews that touch controllers, DTOs, or OpenAPI YAML
- Migrations from code-first annotation sprawl to a maintained contract under `openapi/`
- Client or partner integration work where a breaking schema change would ship unnoticed

## Baseline rules
1. **Contract first.** Keep an OpenAPI 3.0/3.1 document in the repo (e.g. `openapi/openapi.yaml`). Treat it as the source of truth for paths, methods, status codes, media types, and schemas. Generate or hand-write controllers and DTOs to match — do not invent fields in Java that are absent from the spec (or vice versa).
2. **springdoc (or equivalent) stays honest.** Prefer springdoc-openapi to serve `/v3/api-docs` and Swagger UI from the running app. If you use annotation overlays (`@Operation`, `@Schema`), they must not contradict the YAML. Fail CI when the served document drifts from the committed contract (diff against a golden file or an openapi-diff step).
3. **DTOs match schemas.** Map every request/response schema to a dedicated record/class. Use Jakarta Bean Validation (`@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Email`, `@Pattern`, `@Valid` on nested objects) that mirrors `required`, `minLength`/`maxLength`, `pattern`, and `format` in the OpenAPI schema. Prefer records or immutable types; avoid exposing JPA entities on the wire.
4. **Controllers are thin.** `@RestController` methods accept/return DTOs only, declare explicit `@RequestMapping`/`@GetMapping` paths and produces/consumes, and map to the versioned base path from the contract (`/api/v1/...`). No business logic in the controller — delegate to a service.
5. **Errors are `application/problem+json`.** Enable Spring Problem Details (`spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` or WebFlux equivalent). Use `@RestControllerAdvice` returning `ProblemDetail` (or a documented subtype) for 4xx/5xx. Document error responses in the OpenAPI with `content.application/problem+json` and a Problem schema — do not leave error bodies as unspecified `application/json`.
6. **Version deliberately.** Put the major version in the URL (`/api/v1`). Additive changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) stay in the same major; breaking changes get a new major and a deprecation window. Never silently rename or remove a required field.
7. **Security and docs endpoints are explicit.** Document auth schemes (`bearer`, OAuth2) in the OpenAPI `components.securitySchemes` and apply them per operation. If Swagger UI / `/v3/api-docs` are exposed, gate them behind profile or Spring Security rules appropriate for the environment (see actuator hardening for management-port patterns).
8. **Instruction files for coding agents.** Keep path-scoped Copilot instructions on controllers and OpenAPI YAML; a Claude skill for this checklist; and an AGENTS.md OpenAPI section so agents regenerate or edit against the contract instead of freelancing shapes.

## Review checklist
- [ ] Committed OpenAPI YAML covers every public endpoint (path, method, status, media type)
- [ ] Request/response DTOs and Bean Validation match schema `required` / constraints
- [ ] Controllers use versioned base path; no entity leak onto the API
- [ ] Error responses documented and returned as `application/problem+json`
- [ ] CI fails on contract drift (golden `/v3/api-docs` or openapi-diff)
- [ ] Security schemes declared; docs UI not wide-open in production
- [ ] Agent instruction files point at controllers + OpenAPI paths

## Anti-patterns
- Returning JPA entities or `Map<String,Object>` from controllers
- `@ApiResponse` / springdoc annotations that disagree with the committed YAML
- Undocumented 500 HTML error pages or ad-hoc `{ "message": "..." }` JSON
- Breaking field renames without a `/api/v2` and a deprecation note

# Skill: LLM Eval CI Regression Gate

## Goal
Every change that can move model behaviour — prompt text, model or deployment version, retrieval settings, tool schemas, or the code around them — is scored against a versioned golden set in CI, and the pull request fails only on a real regression, not on sampling noise.

## When to apply
- Repos that ship LLM features (RAG, classifiers, extractors, agents) with prompts or model config under version control
- Adding or tightening an eval job in GitHub Actions or Jenkins for a Python eval harness (pytest, a custom runner, or an existing eval CLI)
- Reviews of PRs that touch `prompts/`, model/deployment names, temperature, retrieval top-k, or tool definitions

## Baseline rules
1. **Golden set lives in Git.** Keep cases in `evals/golden/*.jsonl` with a stable `id`, `input`, expected output or reference, and `tags` (happy-path, edge, safety, past-incident). Version the set; changing it is a reviewed PR, never a side effect of a feature change. No real customer data or PII/PHI — synthesize or redact.
2. **Two tiers.** A PR tier (roughly 50–200 cases, minutes, bounded cost) runs on pull requests; a full tier (hundreds or more, multi-sample) runs nightly and before release. Trigger the PR tier with path filters on prompts, model config, eval code, and the LLM client package.
3. **Deterministic checks block; judges earn their way in.** Schema/JSON validity, required fields, exact-match labels, regex or allow-list checks, refusal on safety cases, and latency/token budgets are hard gates. LLM-as-judge metrics start as warnings until they agree with a human-labelled sample; then use a binary pass/fail rubric with structured JSON output, not a 1–10 score.
4. **Pin everything that moves.** Pin the model/deployment version (and the judge's), API version, temperature, seed where supported, dataset version, and harness version. Record them in the results file so a diff in scores can be traced to a diff in config.
5. **Compare to a baseline, keep a floor.** Commit `evals/baseline.json` with per-metric aggregates from the last accepted run. Fail when a metric drops more than its tolerance below baseline **or** falls under an absolute floor (safety metrics: floor only, zero tolerance). Updating the baseline is its own reviewed commit with before/after numbers.
6. **Respect the noise floor.** Run each non-deterministic case N times (3–5 on PRs) and aggregate. On small sets, judge pass-rate deltas with a Wilson interval or a paired comparison against the base branch rather than a raw point difference — a few points on 50 cases is usually noise.
7. **Gate wiring is least-privilege.** The eval job sets explicit `permissions:` (`contents: read`, plus `pull-requests: write` only if it comments), prefers OIDC to Azure over long-lived keys, reads provider secrets from the environment, and never runs secret-bearing evals on untrusted fork code. Set a timeout and a per-run spend cap; make the job a required status check.
8. **Evidence on every run.** Write a machine-readable results file (per-case outcome, scores, config pins), upload it as an artifact, and print a short Markdown summary to the job summary: metric, baseline, candidate, delta, verdict, and the worst failing case ids. Exit non-zero on regression.
9. **Instruction files for coding agents.** Agents editing prompts or model config must run the PR tier locally (or say why they could not), must not edit the golden set or baseline in the same change, and must report the delta table.

## Review checklist
- [ ] Golden set versioned in Git, tagged, free of real PII/PHI
- [ ] PR tier path-filtered and bounded; full tier scheduled
- [ ] Deterministic checks are blocking; judge metrics calibrated or warn-only
- [ ] Model, judge, temperature, seed, dataset, and harness versions pinned and recorded
- [ ] Baseline file + per-metric tolerance + absolute floors; safety has zero tolerance
- [ ] Multi-sample aggregation; small-set deltas judged with an interval, not a point diff
- [ ] Workflow `permissions:` minimal, OIDC or env secrets, no secrets on fork PRs, timeout + spend cap
- [ ] Results artifact + job summary; non-zero exit on regression; required check enabled
- [ ] Agent instructions forbid editing golden set/baseline alongside prompt changes

## Example layout
```
evals/
  golden/core.jsonl        # versioned cases
  baseline.json            # accepted per-metric aggregates
  gate.py                  # compare results vs baseline, exit 1 on regression
  config.yaml              # model, judge, temperature, seed, samples, tolerances
.github/workflows/llm-eval.yml
```

## Gate policy sketch (`evals/config.yaml`)
```yaml
samples_per_case: 3
metrics:
  json_valid:      { floor: 1.00, tolerance: 0.00, blocking: true }
  label_accuracy:  { floor: 0.85, tolerance: 0.03, blocking: true }
  safety_refusal:  { floor: 1.00, tolerance: 0.00, blocking: true }
  judge_faithful:  { floor: 0.75, tolerance: 0.05, blocking: false }  # warn until calibrated
```

## Tool placement
- **GitHub Copilot:** path-scoped `.github/instructions/llm-eval.instructions.md` with `applyTo: "prompts/**,evals/**,**/llm/**"`; optionally the same checklist as `.github/skills/llm-eval-ci-regression-gate/SKILL.md`.
- **Claude Code:** `.claude/skills/llm-eval-ci-regression-gate/SKILL.md` (frontmatter `name`, `description`) plus one CLAUDE.md line: prompt/model changes must pass `evals/gate.py`; never edit golden set or baseline in the same PR.
- **Codex:** an "LLM evals" section in root `AGENTS.md`, or a nested `evals/AGENTS.md` that applies to that subtree.

## Anti-patterns
- A single-sample run with a fixed absolute threshold that flips red on noise and gets ignored
- Bumping the baseline or deleting failing cases in the same PR that caused the drop
- Unpinned "latest" model aliases for the app or the judge
- Judge scores on a 1–10 scale gating merges with no human calibration
- Eval job with `write-all` permissions or provider keys exposed to fork PRs

# Skill: Maven Dependency CVE Hygiene Guardrails

## Goal
Keep Java/Maven dependency graphs pinned, convergent, and continuously scanned so CVEs are caught in CI, fixed with deliberate BOM or override bumps, and never papered over with silent version drift or undocumented suppressions.

## When to apply
- New services or modules adding Spring Boot / platform BOM imports and third-party libraries
- Dependabot, Renovate, or OWASP Dependency-Check / SCA findings on `pom.xml`
- Reviews that mention version ranges, conflicting transitive jars, or "just exclude it"
- Parent POM / company BOM changes that retarget dozens of managed versions
- Release trains where snapshot or dynamic versions must not ship

## Baseline rules
1. **One source of truth for versions.** Prefer a parent POM or imported BOM (`type=pom` / `scope=import` in `dependencyManagement`) for Spring Boot, Jackson, Azure SDK, Testcontainers, and similar aligned sets. Module POMs declare dependencies **without** versions when the BOM already manages them. Do not sprinkle duplicate `<version>` tags across modules.
2. **Pin releases; ban ranges.** Use exact versions (or a single managed property) — never `LATEST`, `RELEASE`, or open Maven version ranges (`[1.0,)`) in production builds. Enforcer `requireReleaseDeps` (and ban snapshots on release profiles) keeps CI honest.
3. **Enforce convergence.** Turn on `maven-enforcer-plugin` with `dependencyConvergence` (and usually `requireUpperBoundDeps`). When two paths pull different versions of the same GAV, fix it with `dependencyManagement` (preferred) or a justified exclusion — do not rely on nearest-wins mediation.
4. **Declare what you compile against.** Anything referenced from source should be a **direct** dependency. Relying on a transitive for compile-scope APIs breaks when that transitive disappears in a BOM bump.
5. **Override after the BOM import.** In `dependencyManagement`, order matters: the **last** matching entry wins. Put CVE hotfix overrides **after** the Spring Boot / platform BOM import so they actually take effect. Document the CVE id and removal criteria next to the override.
6. **Upgrade before exclude.** Prefer bumping the BOM or the managing parent that brings the fixed version. Use `<exclusions>` only when the transitive is unused and an upgrade is blocked — and leave a comment with the ticket/CVE. Blanket exclusions that drop logging or security providers are not a fix.
7. **Scan the resolved tree in CI.** Run OWASP `dependency-check-maven` (or the org's approved SCA: Snyk, Trivy filesystem, GitHub Dependabot alerts) against the **resolved** classpath, not only direct deps. Pin the plugin/action version. Set a fail threshold (for example `failBuildOnCVSS` ≥ 7 or org policy) on PR builds.
8. **NVD / feed reliability.** For OWASP Dependency-Check in shared runners, prefer a mirrored NVD/data feed your platform already operates; document cache directories so every job does not hammer public NVD. A flaky CVE DB is not an excuse to skip the gate — fail closed or use a cached mirror.
9. **Suppressions are temporary and reviewed.** Keep `dependency-check-suppressions.xml` (or tool equivalent) in-repo. Every suppression needs CVE/id, justification, owning team, and a review-by date. Scope suppressions tightly (specific GAV + CVE). Never commit a global "suppress all until date" without an issue link.
10. **Dependabot / Renovate are input, not merge rights.** Enable Maven ecosystem updates; require green CI and a human review for BOM major bumps. Group patch updates when the org allows it; do not auto-merge major Spring Boot jumps without a regression plan.
11. **SBOM when the release process asks for it.** Emit CycloneDX/SPDX from the same reactor CI job that signs the release. The SBOM must match what was scanned — no hand-edited component lists.
12. **Separate app-jar CVEs from base-image CVEs.** Library findings belong in Maven hygiene; OS/base-layer findings belong with container image hardening. Do not close a Dockerfile CVE by tweaking an unrelated `pom.xml` exclude.

## Workflow
1. Inventory: root/parent POM, BOM imports, enforcer rules, existing SCA workflow, suppressions file, Dependabot config.
2. `mvn -q dependency:tree -Dverbose` (or `dependency:tree -Dincludes=…`) for the affected module; locate the vulnerable GAV path.
3. Choose fix: BOM bump → targeted `dependencyManagement` override → (last resort) exclusion + compensating direct dep.
4. Wire or tighten CI scan + enforcer; add/update suppression only with justification.
5. Run unit/integration tests for modules that touch the bumped libraries.
6. PR notes: CVE ids, before/after versions, tree snippet, residual risk (unreachable code, waiting on upstream BOM).

## Tool-specific notes
### GitHub Copilot
- Path-scoped `.github/instructions/maven-dependency-cve.instructions.md` with `applyTo` for `**/pom.xml`, `**/dependency-check-suppressions.xml`, `.github/dependabot.yml`, and SCA workflow YAML under `.github/workflows/`.
- Always-on line in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: versions come from BOM/`dependencyManagement`; no ranges; CVE fixes override after BOM import; suppressions need reason + review date.
- Optional `.github/skills/maven-dependency-cve-hygiene-guardrails/SKILL.md` for agent mode.

### Claude Code
- Procedure in `.claude/skills/maven-dependency-cve-hygiene-guardrails/SKILL.md`.
- CLAUDE.md fact: "Maven versions are BOM-managed; enforcer convergence is required; CVE overrides land after BOM import; Dependency-Check (or org SCA) fails the PR above policy CVSS."
- Before claiming done, show `dependency:tree` path for the CVE and the CI gate config.

### Codex
- Maven supply-chain section in root `AGENTS.md`, or nested `docs/agents/maven-dependency-cve.md` linked from it.
- State: no version ranges, enforcer rules, override ordering, suppression policy, scanner command.

## Anti-patterns
- Version ranges or `LATEST`/`RELEASE` in deployable modules
- Duplicate `<version>` on a dep already managed by the Boot BOM (drift magnet)
- CVE override placed **before** the BOM import (silently ignored)
- Excluding a transitive "to make the scanner green" while still loading it via another path
- Checking in an empty or eternal suppression file with no owners
- Disabling `dependencyConvergence` instead of fixing the clash
- Treating Dependabot PRs as rubber-stamps without reading the tree diff
- Confusing container base-image CVEs with Maven artifact CVEs
- Pinning a vulnerable version forever in a company BOM without a tracked bump

## Verification checklist
- [ ] BOM / `dependencyManagement` is the only version authority for shared stacks
- [ ] No version ranges / LATEST / RELEASE on production deps
- [ ] `dependencyConvergence` (and release `requireReleaseDeps`) enforced

# Skill: AKS HPA Requests & Limits Guardrails

## Goal
Make AKS Deployments scale predictably: every container has honest CPU/memory requests, limits are chosen on purpose, and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler reacts to the signal that actually tracks load — without flapping, starving the node pool, or fighting other autoscalers.

## When to apply
- Adding or editing a Deployment, StatefulSet, Helm values block, or `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` (`autoscaling/v2`)
- HPA shows `<unknown>` targets, never scales, or scales up and down every few minutes
- Pods stuck `Pending` (insufficient cpu/memory) or `OOMKilled` / CPU-throttled under normal traffic
- Namespace ResourceQuota rejections or LimitRange defaults silently changing pod specs
- Right-sizing after a load test, incident, or cost review on AKS node pools

## Baseline rules
1. **Requests on every container.** Set `resources.requests.cpu` and `resources.requests.memory` on app containers, sidecars, and init containers. HPA resource metrics are computed as a percentage of the **request**, so a missing request means the HPA cannot compute utilization (or uses a LimitRange default that nobody chose). Treat a missing request as a bug, not a style nit.
2. **Pick the QoS class deliberately.**
   - **Burstable** (requests < limits) is the default for most HTTP APIs and workers: it packs nodes efficiently and absorbs short spikes. Keep the memory limit close to the request (memory is not compressible — overshoot means OOMKill), and give CPU modest headroom or omit the CPU limit if the platform policy allows it.
   - **Guaranteed** (requests == limits for both CPU and memory) only for latency-critical or noisy-neighbor-sensitive workloads. It buys stable scheduling and eviction priority at the cost of idle reserved capacity and CFS throttling at the limit.
   - Write the chosen class and the reason in a manifest comment or values file.
3. **No BestEffort in prod.** Pods with no requests/limits are evicted first and break ResourceQuota accounting. Namespaces with quotas should reject them; do not work around it by deleting the quota.
4. **HPA only where horizontal scaling is real.** The workload must be mostly stateless (or shard-aware), tolerate extra replicas, and start fast enough to matter. For prod set `minReplicas >= 2` (pair with a PodDisruptionBudget) and set `maxReplicas` with headroom you have actually checked against node pool size, Cluster Autoscaler max node count, subnet/IP limits (Azure CNI), and downstream connection limits such as database pools.
5. **Start CPU targets around 60–80%.** `averageUtilization` in that band leaves room for the scale-up lag (metrics scrape + pod start + readiness). Go lower for spiky traffic or slow-starting JVMs, higher for smooth batch-like load. Memory-based scaling is rarely a good primary signal for runtimes that do not release heap — prefer it only as a secondary metric.
6. **Use the real signal when CPU is not it.** If queue depth, consumer lag, or requests-per-second drives load, scale on custom/external metrics (Prometheus adapter, Azure Monitor) or KEDA scalers (Service Bus, Event Hubs, Kafka, HTTP). KEDA owns the HPA it creates — do not also hand-write an HPA for the same Deployment.
7. **Do not let VPA and HPA fight.** Never run VPA in `Auto`/`Recreate`/`InPlace` update mode on the same CPU/memory metrics an HPA scales on. VPA in `updateMode: "Off"` (recommendation-only) is fine and a good input for request sizing.
8. **Probes gate useful capacity.** New replicas only help once they are Ready. Wire readiness and startup probes correctly — follow `k8s-probes-graceful-shutdown-guardrails` rather than re-deriving probe rules here.
9. **Tune scale behavior to avoid flapping.** Use `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` (default 300s; raise for bursty traffic) and `scaleDown.policies` that cap how many pods or what percent can go per period. Allow faster `scaleUp` with a short or zero window. Scale-up lag on AKS includes node provisioning when Cluster Autoscaler must add nodes — budget minutes, not seconds.
10. **Respect ResourceQuota and LimitRange.** Check the namespace's quota (`requests.cpu`, `requests.memory`, `limits.*`, pod count) against `maxReplicas × per-pod requests`. Know what LimitRange defaults and min/max apply so manifest values are not silently overridden or rejected at admission.
11. **Document where the numbers came from.** Record the evidence next to the values: load-test result, VPA recommendation, or observed p95 CPU/memory from Container Insights / Prometheus over a representative window. "Copied from another service" is not evidence.
12. **Keep Helm and raw manifests in sync.** Resources and HPA settings live in values (per environment) with sane chart defaults; templates must not drop requests when a value is unset.

## Workflow
1. Inventory: containers (incl. sidecars/init), current requests/limits, QoS class, HPA spec/behavior, PDB, LimitRange, ResourceQuota, node pool SKU and autoscaler bounds.
2. Measure: `kubectl top pods`, Container Insights or Prometheus p95/p99 over at least a week of normal traffic, plus a load test where possible.
3. Size requests from steady-state p95 plus small headroom; set memory limit from peak plus safety margin; decide CPU limit by policy.
4. Choose metric and target; set min/max with quota and node capacity math shown.
5. Add `behavior` for scale-down stabilization; verify with a load ramp and `kubectl describe hpa`.

## Anti-patterns
- HPA on a Deployment whose containers have no CPU request
- Sidecar with no requests making utilization math wrong for the whole pod
- `maxReplicas: 100` with a 3-node pool and no Cluster Autoscaler
- `minReplicas: 1` for a prod API with a PDB of `minAvailable: 1`
- CPU limit equal to a tiny request on a JVM service (throttling at startup, slow readiness)
- Memory limit far above request ("burst" that ends in node-pressure eviction)
- VPA `Auto` mode plus CPU HPA on the same workload
- Hand-written HPA alongside a KEDA ScaledObject for the same target
- Scaling on memory for a heap-retaining runtime and never scaling down
- Deleting or inflating ResourceQuota to make a rollout pass

## Tool placement notes
### GitHub Copilot
- Path-scoped `.github/instructions/aks-hpa-requests-limits.instructions.md` with `applyTo` covering `**/k8s/**/*.yaml`, `**/manifests/**/*.yaml`, `**/charts/**/templates/**/*.yaml`, `**/charts/**/values*.yaml`, and `**/*hpa*.yaml`.
- Optional `.github/skills/aks-hpa-requests-limits-guardrails/SKILL.md` for agent mode.

### Claude Code
- Procedure in `.claude/skills/aks-hpa-requests-limits-guardrails/SKILL.md`.
- One CLAUDE.md fact: "HPA utilization targets assume every container sets CPU/memory requests; never add an HPA without them."

### Codex
- An autoscaling section in root `AGENTS.md`, or `docs/agents/aks-hpa-requests-limits.md` linked from it, listing the request/limit policy, target band, and verification commands.

Pair with `k8s-probes-graceful-shutdown-guardrails` (readiness/termination) and `aks-workload-hardening` (security context, pod security) — this skill covers sizing and autoscaling only.

## Review checklist
- [ ] Every container (incl. sidecars/init) has CPU and memory requests
- [ ] QoS class is intentional and documented; no BestEffort in prod
- [ ] Memory limit set from observed peak; CPU limit follows platform policy
- [ ] HPA metric matches the real load signal (CPU, custom, or KEDA)
- [ ] `minReplicas >= 2` in prod; `maxReplicas` fits quota, node pool, and CA bounds
- [ ] No VPA update mode on the same metrics; KEDA and HPA not doubled up
- [ ] Scale-down stabilization/policies set; ramp test shows no flapping
- [ ] Evidence for the numbers recorded in the PR or values comments

---

Follow AKS HPA Requests & Limits Guardrails: requests everywhere, evidence-based sizing, intentional QoS, minReplicas >= 2 in prod, maxReplicas within quota and autoscaler bounds, and stabilized scale-down.
```

# Skill: Spark Job Performance Tuning Guardrails

## Goal
Make Spark / PySpark / Spark SQL batch jobs faster and cheaper by fixing what the physical plan and Spark UI actually show — shuffle volume, skew, spill, join strategy, and file layout — instead of guessing at cluster size or pasting config snippets.

## When to apply
- A job breaches its SLA, runs noticeably slower after a data-volume jump, or costs more than its peers
- Spark UI shows one or two straggler tasks, heavy spill, huge shuffle read/write, or thousands of tiny tasks
- Reviews of new joins, aggregations, window functions, UDFs, or `MERGE`/upsert logic on large tables
- Jobs that write many small files or one giant file per partition
- Someone proposes "just double the workers" or adds `.cache()` / `.repartition()` without evidence

## Baseline rules
1. **Measure before tuning.** Capture a baseline run: wall time, stage durations, input/shuffle/spill bytes, task-duration distribution (median vs max), and cluster cost. Every change is compared to that baseline on representative data — same volume, skew, and file layout as production.
2. **Read the plan first.** Use `df.explain(mode="formatted")` (or `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` / `EXPLAIN COST`) and the SQL tab of the Spark UI. Find each `Exchange` (shuffle), the join type chosen (`BroadcastHashJoin`, `SortMergeJoin`, `ShuffledHashJoin`), and whether filters and column pruning reach the scan.
3. **Keep AQE on.** Adaptive Query Execution (default since Spark 3.2) coalesces small post-shuffle partitions, converts eligible sort-merge joins to broadcast at runtime, and splits skewed join partitions. Do not disable it to "stabilize" a job; tune its thresholds instead (`advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`, skew factor and threshold).
4. **Shrink data early.** Filter and project before joins and aggregations; read only needed columns from columnar formats; make sure partition filters and predicate pushdown appear in the scan node. Avoid `select *` across big tables and avoid exploding arrays before filtering.
5. **Pick the join strategy deliberately.** Broadcast only a side that is reliably small after filtering (and within executor/driver memory) — use a `broadcast()` hint when the size is known and stable. Never broadcast a table that grows with business volume. For large–large joins, align keys and types so Spark does not add casts or extra shuffles.
6. **Treat skew explicitly.** Confirm skew in the stage view (max task time or shuffle read far above the 75th percentile). Let AQE skew-join handling cover sort-merge joins first; for skew it cannot see (aggregations, broadcast joins, sub-threshold hot keys) use pre-aggregation, isolating hot keys, or salting — and document the hot keys.
7. **Size partitions by bytes, not habit.** Aim for roughly 100–200 MB of input per shuffle partition; let AQE coalesce from a deliberately high initial partition count rather than hard-coding `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=200` forever. Use `repartition` only when you need a key-based distribution; use `coalesce` to reduce partitions without a full shuffle.
8. **Spill is a signal.** Large memory or disk spill means partitions are too big or rows too wide. Fix partitioning or row width first; raise executor memory only when the data per task is already sensible.
9. **Cache only reused results.** `cache()`/`persist()` a DataFrame only when it is reused by more than one action and fits comfortably; `unpersist()` when done. Never cache "just in case" and never cache before a filter.
10. **Prefer built-ins over Python UDFs.** Use Spark SQL functions first; if Python logic is unavoidable use pandas/Arrow UDFs instead of row-at-a-time UDFs. No `collect()`/`toPandas()` on unbounded data, and no driver-side loops that trigger one job per item.
11. **Write files of healthy size.** Control output layout so files land roughly in the 128 MB–1 GB range: use the `REBALANCE` hint or `repartition` by the write partition columns, avoid high-cardinality partition columns, and schedule compaction (`OPTIMIZE` / auto-compaction or the table format's equivalent) for incrementally written tables.
12. **Keep statistics fresh.** Run `ANALYZE TABLE … COMPUTE STATISTICS` (or rely on the table format's stats) so the optimizer's size estimates — and therefore join choices — are realistic.
13. **Config changes live in code, scoped and explained.** Set tuning configs in the job definition (session config, job JSON, or asset bundle) with a comment stating the evidence. No cluster-wide overrides to fix a single job; no copy-pasted config blocks with unknown origin.

## Workflow
1. Inventory: job entrypoint, input tables and sizes, output table and its partitioning, cluster/pool definition, current Spark configs, last few run durations.
2. Baseline run on representative data; save the plan and the top three slowest stages with their metrics.
3. Diagnose each slow stage: shuffle bytes, skew (max vs p75), spill, task count, scan pruning.
4. Apply one change at a time in priority order: prune/filter → join strategy → skew handling → partition sizing → write layout → caching → cluster size.
5. Re-run, compare against baseline, and keep only changes that measurably help.
6. PR notes: before/after metrics table, plan excerpts, configs added with rationale, residual risks (data growth, broadcast size drift).

## Tool-specific notes
### GitHub Copilot
- Path-scoped `.github/instructions/spark-job-tuning.instructions.md` with `applyTo` for job code and configs (for example `**/jobs/**/*.py`, `**/src/**/*.scala`, `**/*.sql`, `**/notebooks/**/*.py`, `**/databricks.yml`, `**/resources/**/*.yml`).
- Always-on line in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: "Spark changes need a plan excerpt and before/after stage metrics; keep AQE on; no unbounded `collect()`/`toPandas()`."
- Optional `.github/skills/spark-job-tuning-guardrails/SKILL.md` for agent mode.

### Claude Code
- Procedure in `.claude/skills/spark-job-tuning-guardrails/SKILL.md`.
- CLAUDE.md fact: "Spark tuning is evidence-based: baseline → plan → one change at a time; AQE stays enabled; configs are set per job with a comment."
- Before claiming done, show the `explain` output for the changed query and the before/after metrics.

### Codex
- A Spark performance section in root `AGENTS.md`, or nested `AGENTS.md` under the jobs directory (or linked `docs/agents/spark-job-tuning.md`).
- State: how to run a job locally or on a dev cluster, where plans and run metrics are saved, banned patterns (row UDFs, unbounded collect, blanket cache), and the config-in-code rule.

## Anti-patterns
- Doubling cluster size before reading the plan
- Disabling AQE or hard-coding `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` without measuring
- Broadcasting a dimension table that quietly grows past memory
- Salting every join "for safety" when there is no skew
- `.cache()` sprinkled across a pipeline with no `unpersist()`
- Row-at-a-time Python UDFs where a built-in function exists
- `collect()`/`toPandas()` on full tables inside production jobs
- Partitioning output by a high-cardinality column (user id, timestamp) and creating millions of tiny files
- Benchmarking on a tiny sample whose skew and file layout look nothing like production

## Verification checklist
- [ ] Baseline and post-change metrics captured on representative data
- [ ] Plan reviewed: shuffles, join strategies, and scan pruning explained
- [ ] AQE enabled; any threshold changes justified
- [ ] Skew confirmed (or ruled out) from stage metrics, with the fix documented
- [ ] Spill eliminated or explained
- [ ] No unbounded `collect()`/`toPandas()` and no avoidable Python row UDFs
- [ ] Output files in a healthy size range; compaction plan in place
- [ ] Configs live in the job definition with comments
- [ ] PR includes before/after table and residual risks

description: Use when a Spark, PySpark, or Spark SQL job is slow, spills, has straggler tasks, writes small files, or a review touches large joins and aggregations. Tune from the plan and Spark UI metrics with AQE on, one change at a time.
---

Follow Spark Job Performance Tuning Guardrails: baseline first, read the physical plan, keep AQE on, prune early, choose joins deliberately, handle skew explicitly, size partitions by bytes, cache only reused data, prefer built-ins over Python UDFs, write healthy file sizes, and keep tuning configs in code with evidence.
```

# Skill: Jenkins Declarative Pipeline Guardrails

## Goal
Keep Jenkinsfiles short, predictable, and safe: Declarative syntax as thin glue, real build logic in scripts and build tools, ephemeral agents, bounded runs, secrets that never leak into logs or Groovy strings, and pinned shared libraries — so the controller stays healthy and every build can be reproduced.

## When to apply
- Writing a new `Jenkinsfile` or converting a freestyle / Scripted job to Declarative
- Reviews that add stages, `script {}` blocks, credentials, `input` gates, `parallel`/`matrix`, or a new `@Library`
- Builds that hang, queue forever, fill the controller disk, or slow the whole Jenkins instance
- Moving builds from static VMs to Kubernetes pod agents (for example on AKS)
- Someone asks for a script approval or wants to call `Jenkins.instance` from a pipeline

## Baseline rules
1. **Pipeline as code, Declarative first.** The `Jenkinsfile` lives in the repo next to the code and is reviewed like code. Use Declarative `pipeline {}`; keep `script {}` blocks to a few lines and move anything bigger into a versioned shared library or a shell script.
2. **Groovy is glue, not the build.** Pipeline Groovy runs on the controller. Put compilation, tests, packaging, and parsing in `sh` steps that call scripts or build tools (`./mvnw -B -ntp verify`, `make`, `./scripts/deploy.sh`). Combine many tiny `sh` calls into one script; avoid `JsonSlurper`/`XmlSlurper`, big loops, and file processing in Groovy — use `readJSON`/`readYaml` (Pipeline Utility Steps) or do it in the script.
3. **Never build on the controller.** The built-in node has zero executors. Select agents by explicit `label`, or define a pod template / container image per stage. Prefer ephemeral agents (Kubernetes or cloud agents) so every build starts clean and nothing persists between jobs.
4. **Pin the toolchain.** Use container images pinned by tag or digest, or `tools { jdk 'jdk-21'; maven 'maven-3.9' }` with names that map to fixed versions. Commit the Maven/Gradle wrapper. No "latest" images and no reliance on whatever happens to be installed on an agent.
5. **Bound every run.** Top-level `options {}` sets `timeout(...)`, `buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '30', artifactNumToKeepStr: '5'))`, `timestamps()`, and `disableConcurrentBuilds(abortPrevious: true)` for branch/PR jobs. Remember a stage-level timeout with a stage-level agent includes agent provisioning time — size it accordingly.
6. **Secrets through bindings only.** Use `withCredentials([...])` or `environment { X = credentials('id') }`, scoped to the narrowest stage. Reference secrets inside single-quoted shell strings (`sh 'curl -u "$USER:$PASS" ...'`) so the shell expands them, never Groovy string interpolation (`"${PASS}"`). No `echo` of secrets, no `set -x` around them, no writing them into the workspace or artifacts. Store credentials at folder scope, not global.
7. **Don't punch holes in the sandbox.** No `Jenkins.instance` / internal Jenkins APIs in Jenkinsfiles or libraries, no script approvals that bypass the Groovy sandbox, and no shared-library code that overrides built-in steps like `sh` or `timeout`. If a Jenkins API is truly needed, it belongs in a small reviewed plugin.
8. **Pin shared libraries.** Load with `@Library('team-lib@v2.3.1') _` (a tag or commit), not a moving branch. Libraries are small, tested (for example with JenkinsPipelineUnit), and versioned like any other dependency.
9. **Gates don't hold executors.** `input` (approvals) runs with `agent none` on that stage plus its own `timeout`, so nobody's approval holds a build agent. Use `when { branch 'main' }`, `when { changeRequest() }`, or `when { tag ... }` with `beforeAgent true` instead of `if` logic inside steps. Guard deploys with `lock` and `milestone` so older builds cannot overtake newer ones.
10. **Parallelism with intent.** Use `parallel` or `matrix` for independent work, `failFast true` when one failure makes the rest pointless, and `stash`/`unstash` only for small artifacts — publish big ones to an artifact repository.
11. **Always report and clean up.** `post { always { junit ...; archiveArtifacts artifacts: '...', fingerprint: true, allowEmptyArchive: true } cleanup { cleanWs() } }`. Test results are published even when the build fails; failure notifications go to the owning team, not everyone.
12. **Untrusted changes get untrusted treatment.** Multibranch / PR jobs from forks must not run a modified `Jenkinsfile` with access to deploy credentials; use the trust settings so fork PRs use the target branch's Jenkinsfile, and keep deploy credentials off PR builds entirely.
13. **Lint before merge.** Validate the Jenkinsfile with the Declarative linter (`jenkins-cli declarative-linter` or the pipeline-model-converter validate endpoint) or a Jenkinsfile Runner check in CI. Pipeline fixes go through a PR, not ad-hoc Replay edits that never reach the repo.

## Workflow
1. Inventory: current `Jenkinsfile`, shared libraries and versions, agent labels or pod templates, credentials IDs used, plugins relied on, and the slowest/most flaky stages from recent builds.
2. Map stages to responsibilities (checkout, build, test, scan, package, publish, deploy) and move heavy logic into scripts or build-tool goals.
3. Apply the rules above in order: agents and toolchain → options/bounds → credentials → `when`/gates → parallelism → post/cleanup → library pinning.
4. Lint the result, run it on a branch (and on a PR from a branch, if multibranch), and compare duration and queue time to previous builds.
5. PR notes: stage diagram, credentials touched (by ID only), agent/image changes, timeouts chosen, and anything that still needs a Jenkins admin (plugins, credential scope, trust settings).

## Tool-specific notes
### GitHub Copilot
- Path-scoped `.github/instructions/jenkins-pipeline.instructions.md` with `applyTo` for pipeline code (for example `**/Jenkinsfile`, `**/*.jenkinsfile`, `**/vars/*.groovy`, `**/src/**/*.groovy`, `**/jenkins/**/*.yaml`).
- Always-on line in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: "Jenkinsfiles are Declarative glue: logic in scripts, agents by label or pod template, timeouts on every run, secrets via withCredentials in single-quoted sh only."
- Optional `.github/skills/jenkins-declarative-pipeline-guardrails/SKILL.md` for agent mode.

### Claude Code
- Procedure in `.claude/skills/jenkins-declarative-pipeline-guardrails/SKILL.md`.
- CLAUDE.md fact: "Pipeline Groovy runs on the controller: keep `script {}` tiny, never interpolate credentials in Groovy strings, pin `@Library` versions."
- Before claiming done, show the linter result and the final `options`, `agent`, and credential-binding blocks.

### Codex
- A Jenkins section in root `AGENTS.md`, or a nested `AGENTS.md` beside the shared library (or linked `docs/agents/jenkins-pipeline.md`).
- State: how to lint the Jenkinsfile, which agent labels / pod templates exist, the approved credential IDs, banned patterns (Groovy-interpolated secrets, `Jenkins.instance`, unpinned libraries, builds on the controller), and the required `post` block.

## Anti-patterns
- `agent any` on a controller that still has executors
- 300-line `script {}` blocks doing JSON parsing and loops on the controller
- `sh "curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}' ..."` (Groovy interpolation of a secret)
- `input` inside a stage that holds an agent for days
- No `timeout`, no `buildDiscarder`, and a controller disk full of old artifacts
- `@Library('team-lib@main')` or implicit-load libraries nobody reviews
- Script approvals granted to make `Jenkins.instance` work
- Fork PRs running a modified Jenkinsfile with production credentials in scope
- Fixing pipelines with Replay and never committing the change

## Verification checklist
- [ ] Declarative syntax; `script {}` blocks small and justified
- [ ] Heavy logic lives in scripts or build-tool goals
- [ ] No builds on the controller; agents by label or pinned pod template/image
- [ ] `timeout`, `buildDiscarder`, `timestamps`, and concurrency policy set
- [ ] Credentials bound per stage; no Groovy-interpolated secrets; nothing echoed
- [ ] Shared libraries pinned to a tag or commit; no sandbox bypasses
- [ ] Approval gates use `agent none` + timeout; deploys guarded by `lock`/`milestone`
- [ ] `post` publishes tests/artifacts and runs `cleanWs()`
- [ ] Fork PRs cannot reach deploy credentials
- [ ] Jenkinsfile passes the Declarative linter
